topic: Research: Docker SBX vs E2B vs Daytona vs gVisor 2026: AI Agent Isolation Compared
keyword: Docker SBX vs E2B Daytona gVisor

key_points: Frames agent isolation as a tradeoff between plain containers, VMs, gVisor, and Docker Sandboxes with microVMs.
Argues containers share the host kernel and Docker socket patterns are risky for autonomous agents, while full VMs impose operational overhead.
Positions Docker SBX as VM-level security with container-like startup speed, per-sandbox Docker Engines, and strict network boundaries.
Compares Daytona and E2B by API philosophy: Daytona for workspace lifecycle and stateful dependency-heavy workflows; E2B for quick code execution setup.
Highlights SDK and language differences: Daytona emphasizes TypeScript/JavaScript, Ruby, and Go; E2B emphasizes Python and TypeScript/JavaScript.
Useful competitor gap: it compares E2B and Daytona but does not bring Docker SBX or gVisor into the same decision matrix.
Covers the wider sandbox-provider category and includes E2B, Daytona, Modal, Vercel, Cloudflare, Fly, and Upstash Box.
Calls out E2B's Code Interpreter/Jupyter-style state and Daytona's speed, broad SDK surface, shared volumes, VNC desktop, MCP server, and GPU sandboxes.
Uses a buyer-oriented 'when to choose which' format that a comparison post can outrank by adding deeper isolation and security analysis.
Reviews code-execution sandboxes by architecture, capabilities, compliance, and use case rather than only latency or price.

States E2B uses Firecracker microVMs for strong kernel isolation and quick SDK integration; positions Daytona around OCI/Docker-compatible persistent sandboxes with fast cold starts and unlimited runtime.
Competing angle is vendor-neutral-seeming category analysis from another sandbox vendor; Docker SBX and raw gVisor still need clearer positioning for agent isolation buyers.
Benchmarks seven providers across developer experience and pricing, including E2B and Daytona but not Docker SBX or standalone gVisor.
Lists E2B as best for quick AI-agent integration, about 150 ms cold starts, and 24-hour Pro runtime; Daytona as full-featured dev environments, about 90 ms cold starts, and unlimited runtime.
Offers a compact comparison-table pattern to borrow, but the reported numbers should be cross-checked against current vendor pricing and docs before publication.

stats.fact: Docker Sandboxes run AI coding agents in isolated microVM sandboxes; each sandbox gets its own Docker daemon, filesystem, and network.

Docker SBX security model uses a microVM as the primary trust boundary; host filesystem outside the workspace, host Docker daemon, host network/localhost, other sandboxes, non-allowlisted domains, and raw TCP/UDP/ICMP are blocked by default.

Docker SBX v0.34.0 was released on 2026-06-26; highlights include kit-source allowlisting, experimental native SSH endpoint, sbx setup onboarding, and several network/policy fixes continuing from v0.33.0.
Docker sbx CLI was free to use, including commercial work; organization governance required a separate paid subscription, according to Docker docs checked on 2026-07-09.
E2B states each sandbox is powered by Firecracker, a microVM for untrusted workflows; E2B also advertises same-region starts under 200 ms and 80 ms, plus up to 24-hour sandbox sessions on Pro.

E2B pricing listed a free Hobby tier with one-time $100 credits, 1-hour session length, and 20 concurrent sandboxes; Pro was $150/month plus usage, with 24-hour sessions and 100 concurrent sandboxes, and default 2 vCPU CPU usage at $0.000028/s.

Daytona docs describe sandboxes as full composable computers for AI agents with a dedicated kernel, filesystem, network stack, allocated vCPU/RAM/disk, and defaults of 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM, and 3 GiB disk; organization max limits shown were 4 vCPUs, 8 GB RAM, and 10 GB disk.
Daytona's homepage advertises sub-90 ms sandbox creation from code to execution, SDK examples in Python/TypeScript/Ruby/Go/Java, and separated isolated runtime protection.

Daytona pricing listed pay-as-you-go CPU at $0.00001400/vCPU/s, memory at $0.00000450/GiB/s, 5 GB free storage then $0.00000003/GiB/s, $200 free compute, and GPU options including H200, H100, RTX PRO 6000, RTX 5090, and RTX 4090.

gVisor is a Linux-compatible userspace application kernel with the runsc OCI runtime; it integrates with Docker and Kubernetes, intercepts application syscalls, and provides a third isolation model distinct from plain policy wrappers and full VMs.
gVisor's Docker quick start requires Docker 17.09.0 or greater, configures runsc as a Docker runtime, and runs containers with docker run --runtime=runsc.

Kubernetes Agent Sandbox states its Sandbox custom resource supports runtimes such as gVisor and Kata Containers for kernel and network isolation, plus scale-to-zero lifecycle management for stateful agent workspaces.

A June 2026 arXiv comparative security study found engine classes separate cleanly across architectural axes, but product pin policy is the dominant operator-facing variable; downstream lag ranged from 0 days to 471+ days to opaque/infinite, and no overall ranking was proposed.
The same arXiv study grouped e2b as Firecracker microVM, gVisor as runsc userspace kernel, and Daytona default deploy path as runc/OCI container via Docker-CE 29.x with runc 1.3.5 bundled.

GitHub API snapshot on 2026-07-09: docker/sbx-releases had 222 stars and latest release v0.34.0 published 2026-06-26; e2b-dev/E2B had 12,904 stars and latest release @e2b/cli@2.13.1 published 2026-07-08; daytonaio/daytona had 72,256 stars and latest release v0.190.0 published 2026-06-23; google/gvisor had 18,729 stars and latest tag release-20260706.0.

angles: Make the core comparison about threat model first, not brand: local coding-agent containment, hosted code execution API, persistent agent computer, and runtime primitive solve different jobs.
Differentiate Docker SBX from ordinary Docker containers: the selling point is a microVM plus a private Docker daemon, not merely running an agent inside a container.
Position gVisor as an isolation primitive/runtime, not a full agent-sandbox product: it is strongest when readers already have Docker/Kubernetes and need a user-space-kernel boundary.
Use the June 2026 arXiv study to challenge simple 'microVM always wins' claims: engine class matters, but downstream pinning, patch cadence, fuzzing, and defaults decide real operator risk.

Contrast E2B and Daytona as workflow choices: E2B is quickest for code-interpreter/API tasks with Firecracker isolation; Daytona is stronger for long-lived, stateful, full-computer workflows and GPU-capable sandboxes.

Call out the hidden risk in every sandbox: workspace mounts, broad egress defaults, credential injection, and install-time kit/package supply chain may matter more than kernel isolation for many agent incidents.
Add a pragmatic buyer matrix: safest local coding-agent sandbox, fastest hosted code execution, best stateful workspace, best Kubernetes/runtime primitive, best self-hosting path.
Trend angle: hyperscaler and platform bundling is compressing the category; independent tools must compete on multi-cloud neutrality, open source/self-hosting, price, or deeper isolation.
